new_statements.quote: 2.3 Stress. There is no fixed stress pattern, although stress commonly falls on the penultimate syllable. • In two-syllable words, stress usually falls on the first syllable, e.g. 'enda, 'wane, 'neta ... but pa'ngae. • In three-syllable words, usual stress falls on the middle syllable, e.g. a'kali, e'ndangi ... But it may fall on the first syllable e.g. 'kenapa, 'pokota ... • In four-syllable words, primary stress falls on the third syllable, with possible subsidiary stress on the first, e.g. peta'kare, imbu'singi ... But: 'alemakai, ku'lumbulyu ... Proper names follow no strict rules of stress. ... 2.4 Tone. Many pairs of words are distinguished by high (H) or low (L) tone.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (717 pp., ANU Open Research, CC BY-SA 4.0; text layer copy alongside). extracted text of PDF pp.11-13 reproduces printed pp.3-5 of the Introduction. Printed p.4, sec. 2.3 'Stress', reads exactly: 'There is no fixed stress pattern, although stress commonly falls on the penultimate syllable.' followed by the four bullets (two-syllable words: first syllable, 'enda, 'wane, 'neta, 'rara, 'pumi, 'kaolyo, 'pyara, 'pilyu but pa'ngae; three-syllable: middle syllable, a'kali, e'ndangi, e'para, ka'rena, la'ngimi, pe'ndoko, ra'kane, but may be first, 'kenapa, 'pokota, 'uruwai, 'rambulyu, 'lasaka, 'kilyipu 'kilyipu, 'kapara 'kapara; four-syllable: primary stress on third syllable with poss…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is penultimate (2-syll initial, 3-syll medial, 4-syll third syllable), but the authors state it is not fixed: a lexical minority of words take initial or other stress, longer compounded verb forms usually stress the fourth syllable, proper names are irregular, and a few pairs contrast by stress position (e.g. 'kyakapya 'he became well' vs kya'kapya 'he became mad'). The language also has a lexical high/low tone contrast illustrated with many minimal pairs; the relation between tone and stress is not discussed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In four-syllable words 'possible subsidiary stress on the first' syllable (p.4). Nothing further.
new_statements.exceptions: Two-syllable pa'ngae (final); three-syllable words with initial stress ('kenapa, 'pokota, 'uruwai, 'rambulyu, 'lasaka, reduplicated 'kilyipu 'kilyipu, 'kapara 'kapara); four-syllable 'alemakai, ku'lumbulyu, pa'kalepa, ya'ngalana; multi-syllabics pya'kalyamano, pi'pyamopape; proper names irregular; dictionary entries note stress-contrasting pairs kyakalyamo (initial vs medial stress = 'recover' vs 'go mad') and kyasilyu (initial) vs kasilyu (second). Grammar sketch: urgent-imperative plurals with -pe/-pi and delayed imperatives with -le take penultimate stress on the verb.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements are about isolated words (citation forms as written in the practical orthography); impressionistic, no acoustic data; tone (H/L) treated separately in sec. 2.4 with no discussion of tone-stress interaction.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kyaka Enga of the Baiyer River valley and Lumusa plateau (Enga Province / WHP border, PNG), which the authors treat as a dialect of Enga; Glottolog lists it as its own language kyak1244 (ISO kyc). Some Sau-dialect words are included in the dictionary but the phonology intro is Kyaka.

sources.note: Intro sec. 2.3 'Stress' (p.4): no fixed stress pattern, but stress commonly penultimate; by word length: 2-syll initial, 3-syll medial, 4-syll third syllable with possible subsidiary stress on first, longer forms fourth syllable; listed exceptions and stress-contrasting pairs (kyakalyamo, kyasilyu/kasilyu); proper names irregular.
